head:
Health · Strength

Muscular strength, the forgotten health insurance

When people talk about health and exercise, they talk about cardio, steps per day, VO2max. Strength is seen as a matter of appearance or performance. Yet studies that followed hundreds of thousands of people link it to lifespan. This article looks at whether that link holds when it is separated from endurance, how far you can trust it, and what you can do with it starting this week.

The problem

The health advice you hear most often is aerobic: walk, run, cycle, move at least 150 minutes a week. It rests on good reasons, and the article “Cardio and lifespan: what the data show, and what they do not show” explains what endurance says about your lifespan. Strength, by contrast, rarely appears in a health check-up. It is measured in athletes, not in ordinary people.

Yet some teams have compared people who do strength training with others who do not, then counted deaths over several years. Others measured strength itself, with the bench press, the leg press or a grip dynamometer, and did the same count. The results point in the same direction, and that is precisely what calls for caution. People who are strong may also be those who move more, eat better, smoke less, or have no illness that weakens them.

Above all, there is a more specific objection, particular to this article: you may already be doing cardio. If strength merely reflected endurance, it would add nothing. So the question is not “is exercise good for you?”, which has a known answer, but what strength adds, at equal endurance.

The question

At equal endurance, is higher muscular strength, or regular strength training, associated with a lower risk of death? And what can be said beyond that simple association?

We proceed in six steps, from the general to the specific: the whole population, the dose needed, independence from endurance, strength measured directly, what the randomised trials show, then the objections. The answer comes next, followed by what you can put in place.

What is at stake

What is at stake goes beyond the gym. First there are the diseases the studies count: all-cause death, but also cancer, heart disease, diabetes. Then there are mental health and bones, which randomised trials have studied (step 5). Finally there is independence, whose link with walking, getting up from a chair and everyday movements is explained in the article “Grip strength, a health indicator” on grip strength: it is not repeated here.

There is a decision at stake. The World Health Organization recommendations ask for strength training at least two days a week for adults.11,12 But the share of the population that meets this is small: for example, fewer than 19% of Australian adults according to the University of Sydney, which cites this figure when presenting the Stamatakis study.3 If strength matters as much as is claimed, not doing any is a missed opportunity, and not only for athletes. If it does not matter independently of endurance, you can stick to cardio and save time.
rest:
Step 1 of 6 · The whole population

In large cohorts, people who do strength training die less

The claim: at the scale of whole populations, doing strength training is associated with a lower risk of death.

The first evidence comes from an analysis of 11 British cohorts (health surveys of England and Scotland, 1994 to 2008): 80,306 adults aged 30 and over, followed through the national death register, with 5,763 deaths.1 The authors compared those who reported doing strength training (in a gym or with body weight, for example push-ups, lunges) with those who did not. They accounted for age, sex, health status, lifestyle habits and level of education, excluded people who already had heart disease or cancer at the start, and ignored deaths in the first two years to avoid counting people who were already ill.2,3

The result: a risk ratio of 0.77 for all-cause death. A risk ratio compares two groups: 1.00 means “the same”, 0.77 means a 23% lower risk. For cancer deaths, it is 0.69, or 31% lower.1

One study is not enough. A meta-analysis (which adds up several studies) gathered ten studies of adults aged 18 to 85, followed for 7 to 17 years.6,7 Doing a little strength training, rather than none at all, is associated with a 15% lower risk of all-cause death (ratio of 0.85, six studies), a 14% lower risk of cancer death (0.86, five studies), and a 19% lower risk of death from heart disease (0.81, four studies).6 This last result is fragile: its confidence interval, the range in which the true value probably lies, runs from 0.66 to 1.00, and therefore touches “no effect”.

In two independent pieces of work, doing strength training is associated with a lower risk of death

Risk ratio (HR or RR): 1.00 = same risk as those who do not do strength training; below that, lower risk. Dot = estimate, line = 95% confidence interval. The grey line for heart disease touches 1.00: this result is not established. Sources: Stamatakis et al., American Journal of Epidemiology, 2018; Shailendra et al., American Journal of Preventive Medicine, 2022.1,6

What this means

In two pieces of work that do not use the same data, people who do strength training have a lower risk of death, by 15 to 23% for all-cause death depending on the study. The effect on cancer is clear in both. The effect on the heart is not established in the meta-analysis. This describes groups, not your own trajectory.

What remains to be seen is how much strength training is needed for this link to appear. That determines what you actually have to do.

Step 2 of 6 · The dose

The benefit appears at a small dose, then levels off

The claim: there is no need to train for hours: the zone of maximum benefit is around 30 to 60 minutes per week.

A meta-analysis published in the British Journal of Sports Medicine in 2022 (Momma and colleagues) brought together 16 studies and more than 500,000 people, with follow-up of up to 25 years.4,5 For all-cause death, seven studies provided 42,133 deaths among 263,058 people: strength training is associated with a 15% lower risk, and the curve is not a straight line. The lowest risk is at about 40 minutes per week. For heart disease (seven studies, 16,056 cases), the reduction is 17%, with a maximum around 60 minutes. For cancer, the maximum is around 30 minutes. For diabetes, the risk falls up to 60 minutes, then the benefit declines.4

The Shailendra meta-analysis, cited above, reaches the same place with other data: in four studies, about 60 minutes of strength training per week is associated with a risk of death lower by about a quarter (ratio of 0.74, interval 0.64 to 0.86). The authors note that the risk reduction diminishes at higher volumes.6 The lead author of Momma adds that a higher volume may call for caution, and that the optimal dose is not established.5

The benefit lies between 30 and 60 minutes per week, then levels off

Each point marks the weekly duration at which risk is lowest in the dose-response analyses reported (7 studies for all deaths and heart disease in Momma, 4 studies in Shailendra). These are curves estimated from few studies, not precise thresholds. Sources: Momma et al., British Journal of Sports Medicine, 2022; Shailendra et al., 2022.4,5,6

What this means

The first step is the most rewarding: half an hour to an hour per week is enough to be in the zone where risk is lowest, in these studies. Two 30-minute sessions make 60 minutes (simple arithmetic). More is not shown to be better, but these curves come from a few studies and from self-reported activity: read zones, not thresholds.

This dose is short, which raises the next question. The people who do these sessions often do cardio too. Does the gain really come from strength, or from the endurance that goes with it?

Step 3 of 6 · Independence from endurance

Strength training adds something to endurance

The claim: doing strength training on top of cardio is associated with a lower risk than doing cardio alone, so the two effects are not the same thing.

In the Stamatakis cohorts, meeting the strength training recommendation alone (two sessions a week or more) corresponds to a risk ratio of 0.79 for all-cause death. Meeting only the aerobic recommendation (150 minutes a week of moderate activity) corresponds to 0.84. Meeting both: 0.71.1 In percentage of risk removed, that makes 21%, 16% and 29% (calculation derived from these ratios).

The Shailendra meta-analysis gives the same pattern. Compared with those who do neither, the risk of all-cause death is lower by 18% with strength training alone, by 25% with moderate-to-vigorous aerobic activity alone, and by 40% with both.7 The Momma one also finds a cumulative benefit: an all-cause death risk lower by 40% for the combination.4,5

Strength training and endurance do not replace each other: both together give the best result

Shailendra: values reported by the specialist press (18, 25 and 40%), compared with doing neither strength training nor intense aerobic activity. Stamatakis: values calculated here as 1 minus the published risk ratio (0.79, 0.84 and 0.71), so derived. Both studies use self-reported activity, not measurements. Sources: Shailendra et al., 2022; Stamatakis et al., 2018.1,6,7

What this means

Strength training is not a duplicate of cardio. In both studies, the combination does better than either one taken alone. The reverse is also true: strength training does not replace cardio, and the lead author of Momma says so explicitly. For you, this changes the make-up of a healthy week: the ideal is not to choose, it is to have both.

A review of the literature points the same way. Volaklis and colleagues examined 23 articles, including 15 population studies and 8 clinical studies. Their conclusion: strength is inversely and independently associated with all-cause death, including after accounting for physical activity and cardiorespiratory fitness.10 They also state two limits: for cardiovascular deaths, there are too few data, and for cancer, the studies read did not show that low strength predicts it.

So far, we have mostly compared reported practices. An activity questionnaire is a crude measure. The next step looks at strength itself, measured in a laboratory or clinic, and at how endurance was taken into account.

Step 4 of 6 · Measured strength

When strength is measured, the signal remains, and it is concentrated at the exit from the bottom

The claim: strength that is measured, and not only reported, predicts mortality, even after accounting for endurance, and it is mainly being at the bottom of the ranking that costs dearly.

The Cooper Clinic study (Dallas) followed 8,762 men, aged about 20 to 80, for 18.9 years on average, with 503 deaths. Their strength was measured with the bench press and the leg press, as a one-repetition maximum, then ranked in thirds according to their age.8 The chart shows deaths per 10,000 men per year.

The biggest gap is between the weakest third and the rest, not between the middle and the top

Age-adjusted rates. 8,762 men from the Cooper Clinic (Dallas), 503 deaths, mean follow-up of 18.9 years; strength = bench press and leg press, one-repetition maximum, ranked in thirds according to age. Source: Ruiz et al., BMJ, 2008.8

Read the three bars on the left. The weakest third has a rate of 38.9 deaths per 10,000 men per year, against 25.9 for the middle third and 26.6 for the strongest third. The middle and the top are almost identical: the gap opens up between the bottom and the rest. The rate for the middle third is about a third lower than that of the weak third (derived calculation: 38.9 to 25.9). For heart disease and cancer, the slope continues, more gently.

After accounting for age, physical activity, tobacco, alcohol, body mass index, diseases known at the start and family history, the risk ratios are 0.72 (middle third) and 0.77 (strongest third) for all-cause death, and 0.72 and 0.68 for cancer. For heart disease, they are 0.74 and 0.71, but their intervals include 1: this result is not established.8

The decisive point is the adjustment for cardiorespiratory fitness, which stands in for endurance. Once this adjustment is added, the link between strength and all-cause death remains significant, as does the one with cancer. The link with heart disease, however, is no longer significant (probability of 0.23). The authors point out that cardiovascular deaths are few (145), which limits the power of the analysis.8

What this means

This is the shape that the article “Cardio and lifespan: what the data show, and what they do not show” had already found for endurance: the most marked gain is at the exit from the lowest level. If you are at the bottom for your age, the first step counts the most. And strength keeps a link with mortality when endurance is accounted for, at least for all-cause death and cancer in these men.

This cohort is not your population: mostly white, educated and fairly well-off men, and only 383 were aged 60 or over.8 So we need to see whether simple tests, feasible anywhere, give the same signal in many more people.

García-Hermoso and colleagues brought together 38 studies of adults in apparent good health: 1,907,580 people and 63,087 deaths. The strongest grip, compared with the weakest, is associated with a risk ratio of 0.69 for all-cause death, 0.60 in women and 0.69 in men. Knee extension strength gives 0.86. The authors specify that the link holds whatever the age and the length of follow-up, and propose that simple tests be used to identify people with low strength.9

Simple strength tests, grip or legs, are associated with lower mortality

Risk ratio of all-cause death, highest strength versus lowest (1.00 = same risk). Meta-analysis of 38 studies, 1,907,580 adults in apparent good health, 63,087 deaths. Source: García-Hermoso et al., Archives of Physical Medicine and Rehabilitation, 2018.9

What this means

A few seconds of grip, or a leg test, carry a signal across more than 1.9 million people. It is not a diagnosis: the group says something, not your own person. The article “Grip strength, a health indicator” details what grip measures and what it does not measure.

So far, everything is an association: stronger people die less. That is not the same as “getting stronger changes something”. To move towards cause, we need randomised trials, where chance decides who trains.

Step 5 of 6 · The randomised trials

Resistance training changes measurable things, but not mortality itself

The claim: trials in which chance decides who trains show effects on mood, blood sugar and bones, which makes the hypothesis of a causal effect more plausible, without demonstrating it for mortality.

In the work read for this article, no randomised trial measures mortality as a function of strength training. The trials look at intermediate outcomes, which are plausible links. Three examples.

Mental health

A meta-analysis of 33 randomised trials (1,877 participants, mean age 52, programmes of about 16 weeks, most often three times a week) finds that resistance training reduces depressive symptoms, with an effect size of 0.66 (interval 0.48 to 0.83). An effect size of this order is considered medium. The effect also appears in people who are not depressed in the clinical sense (0.45): it is larger in those with mild to moderate symptoms (0.90).13

The methodological detail matters. In trials where assessment was blinded (the person measuring does not know who is training), the effect falls to 0.56, against 1.07 without blinding. The results are also very heterogeneous from one trial to another, and in the analysis, the gain in strength does not emerge as a significant factor in the effect.13

Blood sugar

In people with type 2 diabetes, a report of a meta-analysis of 47 trials of at least 12 weeks indicates a drop in HbA1c (the marker of blood sugar over three months) of 0.57 points with strength training alone, 0.73 with aerobic exercise alone and 0.51 with both combined. Strength training alone rests on only four trials and 261 participants, aerobic exercise on 18 trials and 848 participants.15

Randomised trials show effects on mood and blood sugar, more modest when assessment is blinded

Left: 33 randomised trials, 1,877 participants (Gordon et al., JAMA Psychiatry, 2018). Right: meta-analysis of 47 trials of at least 12 weeks; strength training alone rests on 4 trials and 261 participants, aerobic exercise on 18 trials and 848 participants, the combination on 7 trials and 404 participants (MDedge report).13,15

What this means

Strength training acts on things that matter: mood, blood sugar. But these effects are medium, heterogeneous, and they melt away when trials are better controlled. On blood sugar, strength training is not superior to aerobic exercise in these figures: it is comparable, and the small numbers prevent telling them apart.

Bones

A network analysis of 19 randomised trials (919 postmenopausal women) compared several strength training protocols with no training. The protocol ranked first for bone density is moderate-intensity strength training (65 to 80% of maximum load), three days a week: it improves the density of the lumbar spine and the femoral neck. No difference is significant for the total hip. Neither the participants nor the trainers were blinded in the trials, and only three trials had a low risk of bias according to an assessment tool.14 These results concern postmenopausal women: do not draw a conclusion from them for a 30-year-old man.

What this means

The link between strength and health is not only a population correlation: when people are made to train, measurable things move, which makes it plausible that strength plays a role. But “plausible” is not “demonstrated”: the effects observed remain modest and uneven.

We come to the step where the argument has to test itself: which objections bring it down, and which leave it standing?

Step 6 of 6 · The objections

The serious objections, and what remains uncertain

The claim: the link between strength and mortality withstands the main objections, but it is more modest and more uncertain than the headlines say.

Objection 1: illness makes people weak, not the reverse

A person who is ill, sometimes without knowing it, exercises less and has less strength, and is more likely to die. This is reverse causation. The studies have countermeasures: the Stamatakis analysis excludes people with heart disease or cancer at the start and ignores deaths in the first two years.2,3 The Cooper Clinic authors nevertheless acknowledge that undetected illness remains a concern in any observational study.8 The countermeasure reduces the problem, it does not remove it.

Objection 2: people who train have a healthier lifestyle

That is likely: people do strength training when they look after themselves. The studies adjust for tobacco, alcohol, physical activity, weight. But in the Shailendra meta-analysis, activity is reported by questionnaire, the questions varied from one study to another and activity may have changed during follow-up.7 A questionnaire does not capture everything, and what is not measured cannot be adjusted for. None of these studies can fully rule out this bias.

Objection 3: few studies, results that diverge

The Momma meta-analysis acknowledges a limited number of studies, a possible publication bias (studies that find an effect are more often published, which can inflate the result) and a majority of American studies.4 The results are not uniform: the link with heart disease is clear in Momma (17%) but not established in Shailendra nor, after adjustment for endurance, in Ruiz. For cancer, Stamatakis and Ruiz find a link, Volaklis finds no evidence that low strength predicts cancer death, and Momma finds no benefit of strength training alone on certain cancers (bowel, kidney, bladder, pancreas).1,5,8,10

Objection 4: “health insurance” means protection, and nobody has proved it

The word “insurance” assumes that having strength protects you. Population studies show an association, randomised trials an effect on intermediate outcomes. No work read shows that increasing your strength lengthens your life by a given amount. Momma, moreover, insists that strength training will never replace aerobic activity in the recommendations.4

Objection 5: these people do not necessarily resemble you

The Cooper Clinic follows men, and women are absent for lack of enough deaths.8 Young adults are poorly covered by these sources: what you read applies mainly to middle-aged adults.

What this means

No objection brings the result down, but each one reduces it: the effects are smaller than the raw figures, the cause is not demonstrated, and several sub-results (heart, certain cancers) are disputed. It can be argued that strength matters at equal endurance. No numerical promise can be drawn from it.

The answer to the problem

The question asked was: at equal endurance, is higher strength, or regular strength training, associated with a lower risk of death? The answer is yes, with different degrees of certainty.

What is solid. The association exists. It appears in work that does not use the same data (British cohorts, meta-analyses, the Cooper Clinic), with reported practices as with measured strength, and it always goes in the same direction for all-cause death. Endurance does not explain everything: strength training added to cardio is associated with a lower risk than cardio alone, and strength remains linked to mortality after adjustment for cardiorespiratory fitness in the Cooper Clinic men.

What is probable. The zone of benefit is around 30 to 60 minutes per week, with a ceiling. The gain is more marked at the exit from the lowest level of strength. Real but modest effects are measured in trials on mood, blood sugar and bones, which makes a role for strength itself plausible.

What is not demonstrated. That getting stronger lengthens life by a precise amount; that the benefit on the heart exists independently of endurance; that the gain extends to all cancers; that more than 60 minutes per week is better; that these results hold identically for women, young adults and populations other than those studied.

The expression “forgotten health insurance” is therefore right about the forgetting (strength is little measured and little practised) and too strong about the insurance: an insurance protects by contract, whereas these data show a link without proving it causal.

What to put in place

Here is what the data allow you to do, from the most solid to the most practical. None of it is an individual medical prescription.

  1. Measure your strength, then place yourself.Do the strength test on this page, under the same conditions each time (same time of day, same warm-up). Compare yourself with your age and your sex, not with someone else. A result at the bottom of the ranking is a starting signal, not a verdict.9 For grip in particular, the article “Grip strength, a health indicator” explains how to read it.
  2. Aim for at least two sessions a week.This is the WHO recommendation for adults: strength training at moderate intensity or more, on the major muscle groups.11,12 The Stamatakis cohorts counted body-weight exercises (push-ups, lunges) as strength training, and the University of Sydney indicates that they would be as effective as the gym, which remains an association.3
  3. Stay within a zone of 30 to 60 minutes per week in total.For example two 30-minute sessions (simple arithmetic). The studies read show no gain beyond 60 minutes, and Momma recommends caution beyond that.5,6
  4. Keep your endurance.In the two large studies, the combination does better than either alone, and strength training does not replace cardio.1,4,7 If you already do 150 minutes of cardio a week, add strength training rather than taking some away.
  5. Retest regularly.Every 8 to 12 weeks is a THW practice suggestion, not a duration taken from a study: long enough for a change to be visible, short enough to stay motivating. If you start from the bottom, the first step is the one that counts the most in the Cooper Clinic study.8

If you have a known illness, chest pain or unusual breathlessness, seek medical advice before increasing the load. For postmenopausal women, the bone trials tested three sessions a week at 65 to 80% of maximum load; this is a point to discuss with a professional.14

What these figures do not say
  • These are associations. No work read measures mortality after strength training assigned by chance.
  • Activity is often reported by questionnaire, which is imprecise.7
  • Several results rest on few studies, with a possible publication bias.4
  • The cohort with measured strength is made up of men, mostly white, educated and well-off.8
  • The effects on the heart and on certain cancers diverge from one study to another.

Frequently asked questions

Do you need to lift heavy?

The WHO recommendations speak of moderate intensity or more.12 In the bone trials in postmenopausal women, the moderate protocol (65 to 80% of maximum load, three times a week) is the one that comes out on top.14 Nothing in the studies read shows that lifting heavier lengthens life.

Is body weight enough?

The Stamatakis cohorts counted push-ups, lunges and similar exercises, and the University's communication indicates effects comparable to the gym.3 This is an observational result, not one from a direct comparison in a trial.

Do you have to choose between cardio and strength?

No. In the data read, the combination gives the lowest risk, 40% lower in two meta-analyses, and each one alone brings something.4,7

My strength is at the bottom for my age: is that dangerous?

No, in the sense of a diagnosis. The studies speak of groups. Low strength is a signal to act, and the most rewarding step, judging by the observed shape, is the one that leaves the bottom.8,9
